NQ3 · What brings on the upper-back pain? ASK: “What makes it worse — breathing, coughing, twisting, sitting, lifting the arms?”
Twisting, deep breaths, coughing or rolling in bed — sharp, one-sided, near the spine or along a rib

NT5 · Rib (costovertebral) joint check • Press along the rib where it meets the spine, and along the rib itself: one tender spot that reproduces the familiar pain? • Do a deep breath, a cough, side-bending away and trunk rotation reproduce it? • Spring the rib gently (physio-level). • Re-check N1 and N9 first: chest pain with effort or breathlessness, or a burning band with skin sensitivity, is NOT a rib-joint problem. WHO: anyone trained; physio-level (rib springing)
A local tender rib or joint reproduces the pain

ND10 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Rib (costovertebral) joint pain WHAT IT IS: a sprained or irritated joint where a rib meets the spine — sharp, one-sided pain with breathing, coughing, twisting or rolling in bed, often after lifting, a twist or a bout of coughing. Usually settles over weeks (consensus). NEXT STEP: breathing exercise (slow deep breaths, expanding the sore side into a hand placed on the ribs), gentle rotation and side-bending mobility, then trunk and shoulder-blade strength. AVOID: heavy one-sided lifting and twisting while it is irritable. DANGER: fever, breathlessness, or chest pain with effort → N1. EXERCISE GROUP: NX-B (mobility — breathing branch) STAGE 4 MODULE: upper-back module.
Not reproduced locally → thoracic mobility deficit (ND6)
Sitting, slouching, desk or sewing work — stiff, aching across the mid-back

ND6 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Thoracic (mid / upper-back) pain with mobility deficits WHAT IT IS: aching, stiffness and local pain between or below the shoulder blades, linked with long sitting or bent postures, with stiff, tender thoracic segments and no Stage 1 warning signs. NEXT STEP: thoracic extension and rotation mobility, shoulder-blade strengthening, breathing and posture variety; a physio may add thoracic mobilisation or manipulation. AVOID: long slumped postures without breaks. EXERCISE GROUPS: NX-B (mobility) + NX-C STAGE 4 MODULE: upper-back module.
Older or stooped, with a rounded upper back that’s getting worse (Stage 1 already clear)

ND11 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Stooped upper back — age-related hyperkyphosis, or a stable osteoporotic fracture or Scheuermann’s after clearance (from N8 / N10) WHAT IT IS: a rounded upper back with weak back-extensor muscles, with or without a healed compression fracture confirmed by the doctor, or teenage Scheuermann’s kyphosis confirmed on X-ray. NEXT STEP: spinal-extensor strengthening, posture training, chest-opening mobility, balance and fall prevention. In adults over 60 with hyperkyphosis, 6 months of spine-strengthening and posture training reduced the kyphosis angle compared with health education (Katzman 2017); back-extensor exercise was linked with fewer vertebral fractures (Sinaki 2002). AVOID: loaded bending and twisting of the spine (sit-ups, toe touches). EXERCISE GROUP: NX-F (spinal extensor & bone-safe strength) STAGE 4 MODULE: bone-health module.
Pain in many places — neck plus back, arms or legs; “everything hurts”

NT6 · Widespread pain / central sensitisation check • Clinical criteria (all 3): pain out of proportion to the injury or findings; pain spread widely or not following anatomy; over-sensitive to touch, pressure, cold, light, sound or stress (Nijs 2015). • Central Sensitization Inventory: 40 or more out of 100 suggests central sensitisation (sensitivity 81%, specificity 75%; Neblett 2013). • After whiplash, widespread sensitivity and stress symptoms often travel together — check NT1 risk features. • Re-check N5 (polymyalgia) and N11 (inflammatory disease) in older or morning-stiff patients. WHO: anyone trained (questions); physio-level (interpretation)
Yes — widespread, out of proportion, over-sensitive

ND12 · WORKING DIAGNOSIS: Chronic neck pain with widespread pain / central sensitisation (nociplastic pain) WHAT IT IS: a sensitised nervous system: neck pain plus pain in many areas, flaring easily and out of proportion to any tissue problem; often with poor sleep, fatigue and stress. Real pain — not imagined, and not damage. NEXT STEP: pain education first; graded activity and graded exposure to avoided tasks (driving, overhead work, looking up); regular aerobic exercise starting low and building slowly; gentle neck–shoulder strength; sleep and stress strategies; psychological support (CBT-based) where available. AVOID: repeated scans, collars, long rest after flares, passive-only care, opioids. EXERCISE GROUP: NX-E (graded activity & pain education) STAGE 4 MODULE: yellow-flag module.
No — mainly a neck problem → neck movement check (NT2)

WHY THE LABEL MATTERS (OR DOESN’T) Most neck pain has no single tissue cause you can prove without imaging — and scans often show “wear” in people with no pain. What changes care is the pattern: stiff vs poorly controlled, arm-nerve involvement, headache, whiplash recovery risk, and how widespread and sensitised the pain is. So Stage 2 picks the exercise group, the positions to favour and avoid, and the starting dose. Posture: no single “correct” posture prevents neck pain. Teach variety and breaks, and build the capacity of the tissues for the hours the patient actually spends in that position.

section.name: Neck & upper back · Stage 3 · Exercise groups
section.shape-with-text: STAGE 3 — EXERCISE GROUPS: diagnoses that share a problem share a programme Each working diagnosis points (grey curved arrows) to one or two groups. A group = the shared mechanism + the exercises that target it + how to progress. Pick 3–5 exercises from the group, set the dose in Stage 4, and finish in the CORE PROGRAMME. Why groups work: the neck pain guideline recommends combining mobility, deep-neck-flexor and shoulder-blade training, strength and endurance in most patterns (Blanpied 2017); the emphasis changes with the pattern, not the whole programme.

NX-A · Deep neck flexor & shoulder-blade control For: ND9 cervicogenic headache · ND3 whiplash (after early mobility) · ND4 high-risk whiplash · ND2 posture- and load-related pain · ND7 radiculopathy (once settled) SHARED PROBLEM: the deep stabilising muscles at the front of the neck and around the shoulder blade switch on late and tire early, so bigger muscles overwork and the upper neck is overloaded. • Chin nod (craniocervical flexion) lying on the back, head on a folded towel: a gentle “yes” nod without lifting the head — 10 × 10 s • Progress with a folded blood-pressure cuff under the neck (pressure biofeedback: 20 → 30 mmHg in 2 mmHg steps) if available • Chin nod, then lift the head 2–3 cm and hold 5–10 s • Sitting: chin nod plus gentle hand resistance in each direction (isometrics), 5 × 5–10 s • Shoulder-blade setting — draw the shoulder blades gently back and down, 10 × 10 s → face-down “Y” and “T” arm lifts DOSE: daily, 10–15 minutes; quality over load. EVIDENCE: craniocervical flexion training reduced cervicogenic headache frequency and intensity over 12 months (Jull 2002).

NX-B · Neck & upper-back mobility (move early) For: ND1 mobility deficits · ND5 acute wry neck · ND3 whiplash (early) · ND6 thoracic mobility deficit · ND10 rib joint pain (breathing branch) · ND9 headache (alongside NX-A) SHARED PROBLEM: painful, stiff segments — movement in comfortable ranges calms the pain and restores motion. • Neck turns, tips and nods within comfort: 10 each way, several times a day • Chin tucks (retraction) sitting tall: 10 reps • Thoracic extension over a chair back or a rolled towel: 10 reps • “Open book” rotation lying on the side: 10 each side • Cat–camel on hands and knees; shoulder rolls; shoulder-blade squeezes • Breathing branch (ND10): hand on the sore ribs, 5–10 slow deep breaths expanding into the hand, every hour DOSE: little and often — every 1–2 hours while acute; then 2–3 times a day. PROGRESS: to NX-A or NX-C within 1–2 weeks.

NX-D · Nerve-friendly arm-pain care For: ND7 cervical radiculopathy · ND8 thoracic outlet syndrome · whiplash with arm symptoms (NT1 grade III) SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitive nerve in the neck or shoulder girdle that dislikes being squeezed or stretched. • Positions of ease: hand resting on the head; a pillow under the arm; neck supported in bed • Chin tucks: 10 reps every 2–3 hours, if they ease or centralise the arm pain • Median nerve slider: arm out to the side, palm up; bend the wrist back while tipping the head TOWARD that arm, then release both — 10–15 reps, no stretch pain • Ulnar nerve slider (ND8): make an “OK” sign and bring it gently toward the eye like goggles, 10 reps • Shoulder-blade elevation and retraction; relaxed belly breathing (ND8) • Then progress to NX-A and NX-C RULE: pins and needles or numbness spreading = too much — stop and step down. EVIDENCE: neural mobilisation reduced pain in chronic neck–arm pain (about 1.9 points out of 10; Basson 2017); traction combined with exercise is supported for radiculopathy (Blanpied 2017).

NX-C · Neck–shoulder strength & endurance For: ND2 posture- and load-related neck pain · ND1 mobility deficits (once movement returns) · ND6 thoracic pain · ND8 thoracic outlet (shoulder-blade elevation branch) SHARED PROBLEM: neck and shoulder tissues under-prepared for long hours of static work or repetitive arm use. • Shoulder shrugs holding water bottles or a bag: 3 × 10–12 • Rows with a band, or a towel around a pole: 3 × 10–12 • Reverse fly / band pull-aparts: 3 × 12 • Side raises to shoulder height: 3 × 10 • Wall push-ups → push-up plus (push the shoulder blades apart at the top) • Neck isometrics — hand resistance forward, back and to each side: 5 × 10 s • Work breaks: every 30–45 minutes, 1 minute of movement DOSE: 3 times a week, about 20 minutes; increase the load when the reps get easy (Andersen 2008 ran 10 weeks). EVIDENCE: specific strength training reduced worst neck pain by about 79% in office workers with chronic neck muscle pain (Andersen 2008).

NX-E · Graded activity & pain education For: ND12 widespread pain / central sensitisation · ND4 high-risk whiplash · anyone with a high Örebro score SHARED PROBLEM: a sensitised system, stress and fear of movement — the aim is confidence and capacity. • Pain education: hurt ≠ harm; whiplash and neck pain are not signs of damage; flare-ups settle • Walking or cycling programme: start below today’s comfortable amount, add about 10% a week (by plan, not by pain) • Graded exposure to avoided tasks: driving and shoulder checks, looking up, overhead reaching, carrying • Gentle whole-body strength: sit-to-stand, wall push-ups, rows, carries • Relaxed breathing, a sleep routine, pacing between busy and quiet days DOSE: build toward 150 minutes of moderate activity a week plus 2 strength days (WHO 2020). EVIDENCE: in chronic whiplash, simple advice did as well as a comprehensive exercise programme (Michaleff 2014) — keep the programme simple, active and confidence-building.

NX-F · Spinal extensor & bone-safe strength (upper back) For: ND11 stooped upper back — hyperkyphosis, stable osteoporotic fracture, or Scheuermann’s after clearance SHARED PROBLEM: weak back extensors and a rounded upper back, often with fragile bones — the goals are extensor strength, alignment and fewer falls. • Face-down head-and-chest lifts with a pillow under the tummy: 8–10 reps, hold 3 s • Seated or standing back extension against a wall or chair back: 10 reps • Wall angels; chin tuck with the back of the head toward the wall: 5 × 10 s • Rows and reverse flies with a band • Chest opener: lie on a rolled towel along the spine, arms out, 2–3 min • Balance and sit-to-stand practice AVOID: sit-ups, toe touches, loaded twisting. EVIDENCE: 6 months of spine strengthening and posture training reduced kyphosis in older adults (Katzman 2017); back-extensor strength linked with fewer vertebral fractures (Sinaki 2002); Too Fit To Fracture guidance (Giangregorio 2014).

NX-CORE · CORE PROGRAMME FOR EVERYONE — where every group ends up Once symptoms are settling, every patient moves here. STRENGTH (2–3 days a week, 2–3 sets of 8–12): rows, push-ups (wall → bench → floor), shoulder presses with light loads, farmer carries, plus sit-to-stand or squats for the whole body. NECK–SHOULDER ENDURANCE: deep-neck-flexor holds and shoulder-blade work kept up 2–3 times a week. ENDURANCE: walking, cycling or swimming, building toward 150 minutes a week. WORK AND LIFE TASKS: practise the patient’s own PSFS goals — head-loads and carrying, sewing or computer sessions with breaks, driving and shoulder checks, sleeping comfortably, looking up to hang washing. FLARE-UP PLAN: drop back one level for 2–3 days, use the group’s easing movement (chin tucks, gentle turns), keep active, then rebuild.

section.name: Neck & upper back · Stage 4 · Measure, dose, re-test
section.shape-with-text: STAGE 4 — MEASURE, DOSE THE EXERCISE, RE-TEST Every patient comes here from their exercise group. Everyone gets the same short core battery; the diagnosis adds one module; irritability sets the starting dose; the Örebro score sets HOW the programme is delivered.
NS4-1 · How irritable is the neck? ASK: “Tell me about your last bad flare. What sets the pain off, and how long does it take to settle?” Ask about the last 24 hours, sleep and headaches too.
HIGH: pain at rest or wakes you; small movements flare it; takes hours or until the next day to settle
MODERATE: pain with some activities; settles within an hour or two
LOW: pain only with long or heavy activity; settles within minutes
START GENTLE Positions of ease, NX-B gentle movement, chin nods, short walks, education. Baseline limited to pain, PSFS and the Örebro screen.
START MODERATE Group exercises at full dose and progressive strengthening within the pain rules. Full core battery.
START STRONGER Core programme loading, carrying and overhead work, return to sport or heavy tasks. Full core battery.

NS4-2 · Short-form Örebro Musculoskeletal Pain Screening Questionnaire (10 questions) Scores the risk of long-term disability from pain, beliefs, mood and work factors across any musculoskeletal pain site. A cut-off of 50 identified 83–85% of the people who went on to develop disability (Linton 2011). • Lower risk: advice, reassurance, the group’s exercises at home; few contacts. • Higher risk (50 or more): psychologically informed physiotherapy — tackle fears and beliefs, graded exposure, pacing, goal-setting; involve a counsellor or doctor for low mood or stress-reaction symptoms (especially after whiplash).

NS4-3 · CORE BASELINE BATTERY (about 10 minutes) Needs: a chair, a stopwatch, a phone and a tape measure. Repeat the SAME set at week 0, 4 and 12. 1. Pain 0–10 (faces version for low literacy): average and worst in the last week; arm pain and headache scored separately if present. 2. Patient-Specific Functional Scale (PSFS): the patient names their 3 hardest tasks and rates each 0–10 — this becomes the goal list. Prompt with local tasks: carrying head-loads or water, sewing or computer work, looking up to hang washing, driving or riding a two-wheeler, sleeping, floor work. 3. Neck Disability Index (NDI): 10 items, 0–50 — check for a validated Hindi or Marathi version. 4. Body chart: where the symptoms reach — watch arm symptoms centralise across visits. 5. Neck range: rotation, side-bend, looking up and down (phone inclinometer app, or chin-to-shoulder distance). 6. Deep-neck-flexor endurance hold (seconds). 7. Thoracic rotation in sitting and chest expansion at nipple level (tape measure). 8. Grip strength (dynamometer if available) or a timed bag-carry. 9. Nerve check if any arm symptoms: hand-on-head sign, upper-limb tension test, strength and feeling by root.

NS4-4 · ADD-ON MODULE — pick the one that matches the working diagnosis Neck module (ND1, ND2, ND5): NDI; range of movement; endurance hold; work-break log. Whiplash module (ND3, ND4): NDI, Quebec grade, stress-reaction screen (e.g. Impact of Event Scale), dizziness and concentration checklist. Arm-pain module (ND7, ND8): arm pain 0–10 apart from neck pain; upper-limb tension test; strength and feeling by root at every visit (any new weakness → N6). Headache module (ND9): headache diary (days per month, intensity, medicine days); flexion-rotation range; HIT-6 headache impact questionnaire. Upper-back module (ND6, ND10): thoracic rotation; chest expansion; pain on deep breath 0–10. Yellow-flag module (ND4, ND12, or Örebro 50+): Örebro; Central Sensitization Inventory; PHQ-9 mood screen → doctor if moderate or worse; sleep. Bone-health module (ND11): height to the millimetre; back-of-head-to-wall distance; Timed Up-and-Go; falls in the last year.

PAIN RULES FOR HOME EXERCISE • Pain up to about 5 out of 10 during exercise is acceptable if it has settled back to its usual level by the next morning. If not, hold or step down one level. • Arm-symptom rule: symptoms moving up toward the neck = good; spreading down the arm, or new numbness or weakness = stop that exercise and re-check NT3 / N6. • Dizziness, double vision, or speech or swallowing trouble during exercise → stop at once and go to N3.
NS4-5 · WEEK 1 — dose check ASK: “Did the pain settle back to normal by the next morning after exercising? Have the arm symptoms or headaches changed?”
Settled, arm symptoms the same or better — keep the same level (don’t level up yet)
Not settled, or arm symptoms spreading — step down a level and re-check (NT3)
NS4-6 · WEEK 4 — first re-test Repeat the core battery with the same chair and the same tape. Is it improving? (PSFS, pain, NDI, headache days)
Yes
No
LEVEL UP Add load, endurance time and work-task practice; move toward the core programme. Continue to week 12.

RE-CHECK BEFORE CONTINUING Re-run the Stage 1 safety screen; repeat the arm-nerve check (NT3) and headache screen; re-score the Örebro and yellow flags; physio video exam; doctor review if arm symptoms aren’t improving by 6–12 weeks.
NS4-7 · WEEK 12 — programme review Most change shows by now. Better?
Yes — continue the core programme and move to self-management with a flare-up plan
Still no change after a real trial — revise the diagnosis, refer to a physiotherapist or doctor, consider combined physical and psychological care
